title: Search & the Inverted Index
tagline: How full-text search works under the hood, and why you don't run `LIKE '%query%'` on your database.
summary: Inverted indexes, Elasticsearch, and search as a separate system.

sections.title: Why your database can't do search

paragraphs: Searching text with `WHERE description LIKE '%shoes%'` forces a full table scan — no index can help a leading wildcard — so it's catastrophically slow at scale. It also can't rank by relevance, handle typos, stem words (run/running), or match across fields. Full-text search is a different problem that needs a different data structure: the **inverted index**.
An inverted index maps each *term* to the list of documents that contain it — the inverse of a document→terms layout. Looking up 'shoes' becomes an instant lookup of a precomputed list, not a scan.

blocks.caption: Searching flips the question from 'what's in this doc?' to 'which docs contain this term?' — answered by a precomputed posting list.

items.title: Ingest & analyze
items.detail: Documents are tokenized into terms, lowercased, stemmed (running→run), and filtered (drop stop-words like 'the'). Synonyms can be expanded.

items.title: Build the inverted index
items.detail: For each term, store a posting list of documents (and positions) containing it, plus term frequencies for ranking.

items.title: Query
items.detail: The query is analyzed the same way, then posting lists for its terms are fetched and combined (intersect for AND, union for OR).

items.title: Rank
items.detail: Score matches by relevance (e.g., TF-IDF or BM25: rare terms and higher term frequency score higher) plus business signals (popularity, recency), and return the top results.

blocks.text: Engines like Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (built on Lucene) package all of this — distributed inverted indexes, analyzers, relevance scoring, sharding, and replication — so you rarely build search from scratch. But know the inverted index is what's underneath.

paragraphs: Search runs as its own service alongside your primary database, not inside it. Your source of truth (SQL/NoSQL) handles transactions and exact lookups; the search index is a **derived, denormalized copy** optimized for querying text. You keep them in sync by streaming changes from the DB into the index — typically asynchronously via a queue or change-data-capture (CDC) pipeline.

This means search results are **eventually consistent** with the database (a newly created item may take a moment to become searchable) — almost always an acceptable trade-off. Indexes are **sharded** (split the term space / documents across nodes) and **replicated** for scale and availability, just like databases.

blocks.caption: Writes go to the DB; a pipeline streams changes into the search index, which serves queries.

cheatsheet: `LIKE '%x%'` = full scan, no ranking — never use it for real search at scale.
Full-text search uses an inverted index: term → posting list of documents containing it.
Pipeline: analyze (tokenize/stem/stop-words) → build index → query (combine posting lists) → rank (TF-IDF/BM25 + signals).
Use Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (Lucene) — don't build search from scratch.
Search is a separate, derived, eventually-consistent system kept in sync via queue/CDC; sharded + replicated.

questions.prompt: Explain an inverted index and why it makes search fast.
questions.hint: What does it map, and what does a query become?
answer: An inverted index maps each term to a 'posting list' — the set of documents that contain that term (often with positions and frequencies). It's the inverse of the natural document→terms layout.

It makes search fast because a query for 'shoes' becomes a direct lookup of a precomputed list instead of scanning every document. Multi-term queries combine posting lists (intersect for AND, union for OR), and stored term frequencies let you rank by relevance — all far cheaper than the full scans a `LIKE` query would require.
keyPoints: Maps term → list of documents containing it
Query = lookup precomputed list, not a scan
Combine posting lists for multi-term queries
followUps: How would you support typo tolerance / fuzzy matching?

questions.prompt: Why keep search in a separate Elasticsearch cluster instead of your primary database, and what's the downside?
questions.hint: Different workloads, plus a consistency cost.
answer: Search and transactional storage are different workloads optimized by different structures: the DB gives ACID, exact lookups, and is the source of truth; the search index is a denormalized inverted index tuned for fast text queries and relevance ranking. Mixing them would force one system to do a job it's bad at and couple their scaling. Separating lets each scale and be tuned independently.

The downside is **eventual consistency** and added complexity: you must stream DB changes into the index (via a queue or CDC), so there's a lag before new/updated data is searchable, and you now operate a second stateful system that can drift or fall behind. For search, slight staleness is almost always acceptable, making this a good trade.
keyPoints: DB = source of truth/ACID; index = denormalized for text query+ranking
Downside: eventual consistency (indexing lag) + extra system to operate
Sync via queue/CDC; slight staleness acceptable for search
followUps: How would you re-sync if the search index drifts out of sync with the DB?
